title: MROUND and FLOOR: round to a multiple

screens.prompt: Round each pallet's unit count to the nearest five and put the first one in C2.

hints.syntax: MROUND takes the number and the multiple: =MROUND(B2,5).
hints.func-mround: Rounding to the nearest five is not rounding to a number of decimals — name the multiple instead.
hints.require-ref: Read the count from B2 rather than typing 47 into the formula.
hints.value: 47 is two away from 45 and three away from 50, so the nearest five is 45.
hints.error: Dividing by zero anywhere in the formula leaves #DIV/0! instead of a rounded count.

reject.why: rounds to the nearest whole number, 47, which is not a multiple of five
the right answer from the wrong direction — 45 here, but FLOOR never rounds up
the count typed in, so the second pallet keeps the first pallet's rounding
rounds to the nearest ten, 50, so the packs no longer line up with the fives
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the missing comma means the arguments never separate

screens.prompt: Only whole packs ship, so put the units that fit the full packs of the first order into D2.

hints.syntax: FLOOR takes the number and the pack size: =FLOOR(B2,C2).
hints.func-floor: You need the number of units that a whole number of packs covers, so round down to the pack size.
hints.require-ref: Read units and pack size from B2 and C2, so the second order follows the same rule.
hints.value: Seven packs of six is 42, and the five units left over do not form a pack.
hints.error: Dividing by zero replaces the shipment with #DIV/0!.

reject.why: rounds the pack count to nearest, 48, and commits to a pack nobody filled
rounds up, 48, which is the opposite direction from what ships
the units typed in, so the second order is never actually calculated
rounds to a multiple of one, which leaves the count untouched at 47
rounds down to a multiple of four, 44, using a pack size the supplier never offered
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the missing comma leaves two arguments jammed into one

docs.explain: ROUND answers a question about decimals: how many places do you keep. MROUND and FLOOR answer a different question — what multiple does this number belong to — and the second argument is that multiple, not a count of places. MROUND takes the nearest one in either direction, FLOOR always goes down and CEILING always goes up. This is the arithmetic of packaging: cartons of six, pallets of forty-eight, price steps of five pence. The unit you round to is a real decision, and it lives in the formula rather than in a format, so the number that leaves the sheet is already a whole number of packs. Two traps are worth naming. MROUND ties go away from zero, so 2.5 rounds to 3, and a negative number with a positive multiple is #NUM! rather than a negative answer — the signs have to agree. And a significance of zero makes both functions divide by zero — `=FLOOR(47,0)` is `#DIV/0!`, not 47 — because rounding to a multiple of nothing has no meaning. When the pack size lives in a cell, use it: hard-coding six in twelve formulas means twelve edits when the supplier changes.

errors.text: The multiple was zero, so there is no grid of multiples to round onto.
The two arguments have different signs, so FLOOR cannot decide which multiple to land on.
A multiple arrived as text, so the rounding grid cannot be built.

docs.atWork: A warehouse that ships only whole packs, and a price list quoted in five-pence steps, both computed by formula so the rounding rule is visible and auditable.
docs.outcome: Round to a multiple of something real—a pack, a pallet, a price step—rather than to decimals.
docs.dataset: Pallet counts and order lines packed in sixes
